questions.topic: The Living World and Biological Classification
questions.q: In plants, the taxonomic category equivalent to 'phylum' in animals is called
questions.explanation: Botanists use the term division in place of phylum.

questions.topic: The Living World and Biological Classification
questions.q: The genus name of the human being is
questions.explanation: The scientific name is Homo sapiens; Homo is the genus.

questions.topic: The Living World and Biological Classification
questions.q: Which of the following is the correct way of writing a scientific name?
questions.explanation: The genus begins with a capital letter and the species with a small letter, both in italics.

questions.topic: The Living World and Biological Classification
questions.q: Members of the same species are able to
options: live only in the same place
questions.explanation: A species is a group of individuals that can interbreed naturally and produce fertile offspring.

questions.topic: The Living World and Biological Classification
questions.q: The cat (Felis domestica) and the dog (Canis familiaris) are both placed in order Carnivora. They differ in that they belong to different
questions.explanation: The cat belongs to family Felidae and the dog to Canidae, but both are in the same order.

questions.topic: The Living World and Biological Classification
questions.q: A student writes the name of the human as 'Homo Sapiens Linn.' What is wrong with it?
options: The genus should be written in small letters
The author's name should be omitted always
The species name should begin with a small letter
The name should be in English
questions.explanation: The species epithet must begin with a small letter: Homo sapiens Linn.

questions.topic: The Living World and Biological Classification
questions.q: What is a taxon? Give two examples from the taxonomic hierarchy.
questions.answer: A taxon is a group of organisms of any rank in classification. Examples: the class Mammalia or the genus Homo.
keyPoints: A taxonomic group of any rank
Example of a class or genus
questions.explanation: Each rank in the hierarchy is a taxonomic category; the actual groups are taxa.

questions.topic: The Living World and Biological Classification
questions.q: Why do organisms placed in the same genus share more characters than organisms placed in the same family?
questions.answer: A genus is a lower category than a family. As we go down the hierarchy, the number of shared characters increases, since a genus contains more closely related species while a family includes several genera with greater differences.
keyPoints: Genus is a lower rank than family
questions.explanation: The number of similarities increases from kingdom to species.

questions.q: Which of the following is a liverwort?
questions.explanation: Marchantia is a thalloid liverwort; Funaria, Polytrichum and Sphagnum are mosses.

questions.q: Which of these is a pteridophyte?
questions.explanation: Dryopteris is a fern, a pteridophyte.

questions.q: Bryophytes anchor themselves to the substratum by
questions.explanation: Bryophytes lack true roots and have rhizoids.

questions.q: Which of the following is a gymnosperm?
questions.explanation: Cycas, Pinus and Cedrus are gymnosperms.

questions.q: The prothallus of a fern is
questions.explanation: The prothallus is a small, green, free-living gametophyte that bears gametangia.

questions.q: The sporophyte cells of a fern have 64 chromosomes. How many chromosomes would a cell of its prothallus have?
questions.explanation: The prothallus is haploid and develops from a spore made by meiosis, so it has 32 chromosomes.

questions.q: Write two differences between red algae and brown algae.
questions.answer: Red algae have the pigment r-phycoerythrin, store floridean starch and are mostly marine in warmer, deeper water; brown algae have fucoxanthin, store laminarin or mannitol and are largely found in cold marine waters.
questions.explanation: Their classes are Rhodophyceae and Phaeophyceae.

questions.q: Explain the ecological importance of bryophytes.
questions.answer: Bryophytes are pioneer colonisers of bare rock; on dying they decompose and help form soil for higher plants. They also form dense mats that hold water and prevent soil erosion.
questions.explanation: They play a role in plant succession.

questions.q: The earthworm belongs to phylum
questions.explanation: Earthworms and leeches are segmented worms of phylum Annelida.

questions.q: Which class of vertebrates has feathers?
questions.explanation: Feathers are present only in birds.

questions.q: Which of the following animals has a four-chambered heart?
questions.explanation: Birds and mammals have four-chambered hearts.

questions.q: Lampreys and hagfishes, which lack jaws and have a sucking circular mouth, belong to
questions.explanation: Cyclostomes are jawless vertebrates.

questions.q: Which of the following animals has separate sexes (is dioecious)?
questions.explanation: Ascaris males and females are separate; earthworm and tapeworm are bisexual.

questions.q: Cnidarians exist in two body forms. The free-swimming, umbrella-shaped form is the
questions.explanation: The sessile cylindrical form is the polyp and the free-swimming one is the medusa.

questions.q: Write any three characteristics of phylum Echinodermata.
questions.answer: Echinoderms are marine animals with an endoskeleton of calcareous ossicles, a spiny skin, a water vascular system with tube feet, and adults show radial symmetry; larvae are bilaterally symmetrical.
keyPoints: Water vascular system and tube feet
questions.explanation: Examples include starfish, sea urchin and brittle star.

questions.q: Why is an earthworm called a segmented coelomate?
questions.answer: Its body is divided into many similar segments (metamerism) and has a true coelom, a body cavity lined by mesoderm on all sides.
questions.explanation: Annelids show both metamerism and a true coelom.

questions.topic: Morphology and Anatomy of Flowering Plants
questions.q: The outermost whorl of a flower, made of green leaf-like parts, is the
questions.explanation: The calyx is made of sepals.

questions.topic: Morphology and Anatomy of Flowering Plants
questions.q: After fertilisation, the ovule develops into a
questions.explanation: The ovule becomes the seed and the ovary becomes the fruit.

questions.topic: Morphology and Anatomy of Flowering Plants
questions.q: Pneumatophores, the roots which grow upward out of the mud in mangrove plants like Rhizophora, help in
questions.explanation: They carry out gaseous exchange in waterlogged, oxygen-poor soil.

questions.topic: Morphology and Anatomy of Flowering Plants
questions.q: Lateral meristems, such as vascular cambium, are responsible for
options: increase in length of the plant
increase in girth of the plant
questions.explanation: Lateral meristems cause secondary growth, which increases thickness.

questions.topic: Morphology and Anatomy of Flowering Plants
questions.q: In pea flowers the large standard petal overlaps the two wing petals, which in turn overlap the two keel petals. This aestivation is called
questions.explanation: Vexillary aestivation is characteristic of pea and bean flowers.

questions.topic: Morphology and Anatomy of Flowering Plants
questions.q: The innermost layer of the cortex in a dicot stem, rich in starch grains, is the
questions.explanation: The endodermis, or starch sheath, lies next to the pericycle.

questions.topic: Morphology and Anatomy of Flowering Plants
questions.q: Differentiate between racemose and cymose inflorescences.
questions.answer: In a racemose inflorescence the main axis keeps growing and flowers are borne laterally in acropetal order (youngest at the tip); in a cymose inflorescence the main axis ends in a flower, so growth is limited and the order is basipetal.
keyPoints: Cymose: axis ends in a flower
questions.explanation: Acropetal means younger flowers towards the apex.

questions.topic: Morphology and Anatomy of Flowering Plants
questions.q: Explain how the structure of guard cells makes the opening of a stoma possible.
questions.answer: The inner wall of each guard cell next to the pore is thick and less elastic, and the outer wall is thin. When the cells become turgid the thin outer walls bulge outward and pull the inner walls apart, opening the stoma; when they lose water the stoma closes.
keyPoints: Inner wall thick, outer wall thin
Pore opens or closes with water content
questions.explanation: Guard cells control gas exchange and transpiration.

questions.q: The scientific name of the common frog is
questions.explanation: The Indian bullfrog is Rana tigrina.

questions.q: The scientific name of the American cockroach is
questions.explanation: Periplaneta americana is the common cockroach studied in NCERT.

questions.q: A frog excretes its nitrogenous waste mainly as
questions.explanation: Frogs are ureotelic; urea is made in the liver.

questions.q: The forewings of a cockroach, which are thick, dark and leathery, are called
questions.explanation: Tegmina protect the delicate hindwings; they are the mesothoracic wings.

questions.q: The alimentary canal of a frog is relatively short because the frog
questions.explanation: Carnivores digest protein-rich food easily and need a shorter gut than herbivores.

questions.q: The skin and the lining of the buccal cavity are protected against abrasion by
questions.explanation: Compound epithelium has two or more layers of cells, giving protection from wear and tear.

questions.q: Give two examples each of loose and dense connective tissue.
questions.answer: Loose connective tissue: areolar tissue and adipose tissue. Dense connective tissue: tendons and ligaments (dense regular), or the dermis of skin (dense irregular).
questions.explanation: Cartilage, bone and blood are specialised connective tissues.

questions.q: Why do frogs undergo hibernation and aestivation?
questions.answer: Frogs are poikilothermic and cannot regulate body temperature. To escape extreme cold in winter (hibernation) and extreme heat in summer (aestivation), they hide in burrows and become inactive.
keyPoints: Hibernation in winter, aestivation in summer
questions.explanation: This helps them survive unfavourable seasons.

questions.q: The nucleus of the cell was discovered by
questions.explanation: Robert Brown discovered the nucleus in 1831.

questions.q: The plastids that store starch are called
questions.explanation: Amyloplasts are leucoplasts storing starch; elaioplasts store oil and aleuroplasts store protein.

questions.q: The endoplasmic reticulum with ribosomes attached to its surface is called
questions.explanation: The RER is concerned with synthesis and transport of proteins.

questions.q: Small circular extra-chromosomal DNA molecules found in some bacteria are called
questions.explanation: Plasmids can confer traits such as antibiotic resistance.

questions.q: The movement of RNA and proteins between the nucleus and cytoplasm takes place through the
questions.explanation: The nuclear envelope has pores that allow the transport of macromolecules.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a part of the endomembrane system?
questions.explanation: Mitochondria, chloroplasts and peroxisomes function differently and are not included in the endomembrane system.

questions.q: Write three differences between plant cells and animal cells.
questions.answer: Plant cells have a cell wall, plastids and a large central vacuole, and lack centrioles; animal cells have no cell wall or plastids, have small vacuoles and have centrioles.
questions.explanation: Both have a nucleus, mitochondria and ER.

questions.q: What is the endomembrane system? Why are mitochondria not included in it?
questions.answer: It is a group of membranous organelles whose functions are coordinated and which exchange material through vesicles: endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi complex, lysosomes and vacuoles. Mitochondria are not included because their functions are not coordinated with these organelles.
questions.explanation: Chloroplasts and mitochondria also have their own DNA.

questions.q: The chemical name of table sugar is
questions.explanation: Sucrose is a disaccharide of glucose and fructose.

questions.q: Nearly all enzymes are chemically
questions.explanation: Almost all enzymes are proteins, though some RNAs (ribozymes) also act as catalysts.

questions.q: Haemoglobin is a protein made up of how many polypeptide chains?
questions.explanation: Haemoglobin has four subunits: two alpha and two beta chains.

questions.q: The simplest amino acid, in which the R group is a hydrogen atom, is
questions.explanation: In glycine the R group is H.

questions.q: The enzyme that converts glucose-6-phosphate into fructose-6-phosphate belongs to the class
questions.explanation: Isomerases catalyse the interconversion of isomers.

questions.q: Chitin, found in the exoskeleton of arthropods, is a polymer of
questions.explanation: Chitin is a complex polysaccharide made of N-acetyl glucosamine, a modified sugar.

questions.q: Distinguish between primary and secondary metabolites, giving examples.
questions.answer: Primary metabolites such as amino acids, sugars and nucleotides have known roles in normal growth and metabolism. Secondary metabolites such as alkaloids, rubber, essential oils and pigments have no known direct role in these but are useful to humans or help the plant.
keyPoints: Secondary: not directly involved in growth
questions.explanation: Many drugs come from secondary metabolites.

questions.q: Explain the effect of temperature on the activity of an enzyme.
questions.answer: Activity increases with temperature up to an optimum, as molecules move faster. Beyond it the enzyme is denatured and loses its shape and activity. Low temperature makes the enzyme temporarily inactive.
keyPoints: Rate increases up to an optimum
questions.explanation: The optimum varies, e.g. higher in thermophilic bacteria.

questions.q: One meiotic division of a diploid cell gives rise to how many daughter cells?
questions.explanation: Meiosis I and II together produce four haploid cells.

questions.q: Mitosis is also called
questions.explanation: The chromosome number is the same in the parent and the daughter cells.

questions.q: The longest and most complex phase of meiosis is
questions.explanation: Prophase I has five sub-stages and takes up most of the time of meiosis.

questions.q: The spindle fibres attach to the chromosome at the
questions.explanation: Kinetochores are disc-shaped structures at the centromere.

questions.q: A bivalent seen in meiosis I is made up of how many chromatids?
questions.explanation: A bivalent has two homologous chromosomes, each with two sister chromatids.

questions.q: A cell with 24 chromosomes enters prophase I of meiosis. How many bivalents will be seen at diakinesis?
questions.explanation: 24 chromosomes form 12 homologous pairs, so 12 bivalents.

questions.q: What is interphase? Name its three phases and state the main event in each.
questions.answer: Interphase is the period between two successive M phases. G1: cell grows and prepares for DNA replication; S: DNA is replicated; G2: proteins are made and the cell prepares for mitosis.
questions.explanation: Interphase is the longest part of the cell cycle.

questions.q: Explain how crossing over helps in producing variation.
questions.answer: In pachytene, non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes exchange segments at recombination nodules. This gives chromatids with new combinations of alleles, so that the gametes carry combinations of genes not present in either parent.
keyPoints: New combinations of genes in gametes
questions.explanation: Variation is the raw material of evolution.

questions.q: Leaves appear green because chlorophyll
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll absorbs mostly red and blue light, so green is reflected.

questions.q: The oxygen released during photosynthesis comes from
questions.explanation: Oxygen comes from the splitting of water, shown with 18O experiments.

questions.q: The first stable product of CO2 fixation in C4 plants is a four-carbon acid called
questions.explanation: PEP carboxylase fixes CO2 into oxaloacetic acid in mesophyll cells.

questions.q: Electrons are passed from photosystem II to photosystem I through
options: plastoquinone and the cytochrome b6f complex
questions.explanation: Plastoquinone, cytochrome b6f and plastocyanin carry electrons between PS II and PS I.

questions.q: In Engelmann's experiment, aerobic bacteria collected mostly in the blue and red regions of the light falling on a green alga. This showed that
options: photosynthesis is highest in blue and red light
the alga does not need light
questions.explanation: Bacteria gather where oxygen release is greatest, showing the action spectrum of photosynthesis.

questions.q: Cyclic photophosphorylation takes place mainly in the
questions.explanation: Stroma lamellae have PS I but lack PS II and NADP reductase.

questions.q: List the external factors that affect the rate of photosynthesis.
questions.answer: Light intensity and quality, carbon dioxide concentration, temperature and water supply.
questions.explanation: Internal factors include the amount of chlorophyll and leaf structure.

questions.q: Why are C4 plants more productive than C3 plants in hot, dry regions?
questions.answer: C4 plants fix CO2 efficiently even when stomata are partly closed to save water. Concentrating CO2 near RuBisCO in bundle sheath cells prevents photorespiration, and they have a higher temperature optimum.
keyPoints: Efficient CO2 fixation with partly closed stomata
questions.explanation: Maize and sugarcane are examples.

questions.q: The energy currency of the cell is
questions.explanation: ATP stores and supplies energy for cellular work.

questions.q: Respiration is classified as a
questions.explanation: Respiration breaks down food and releases energy.

questions.q: ATP is formed directly by substrate-level phosphorylation in
questions.explanation: In glycolysis, ATP is made by transfer of phosphate from high-energy substrates.

questions.q: The component of the electron transport chain that contains cytochromes a and a3 and passes electrons to oxygen is
questions.explanation: Complex IV is cytochrome c oxidase.

questions.q: Mature mammalian red blood cells lack mitochondria. They obtain their ATP mainly by
questions.explanation: Without mitochondria, only glycolysis (with fermentation) can supply ATP.

questions.q: The total number of NADH molecules formed from one glucose molecule in glycolysis, the link reaction and the Krebs cycle together is
questions.explanation: Glycolysis gives 2, the link reaction 2, and the Krebs cycle 2 x 3 = 6, so 10 in all.

questions.q: Name the end product of glycolysis and the possible fates of it under aerobic and anaerobic conditions.
questions.answer: The end product is pyruvic acid. With oxygen it enters the mitochondria for the Krebs cycle; without oxygen it undergoes fermentation to lactic acid or to ethanol and CO2.
questions.explanation: The fate of pyruvate depends on the organism and the availability of oxygen.

questions.q: Explain how the electron transport chain and the proton gradient lead to ATP synthesis.
questions.answer: Electrons from NADH and FADH2 pass along the carriers of the inner mitochondrial membrane to oxygen. Energy released pumps protons into the intermembrane space, forming a gradient; protons flow back through ATP synthase, which makes ATP.
keyPoints: Electrons passed down carriers to oxygen
Flow through ATP synthase makes ATP
questions.explanation: This is oxidative phosphorylation.

questions.q: Plants can keep growing throughout their life because they have
questions.explanation: Meristems retain the capacity to divide, giving open growth.

questions.q: The most common natural auxin is
questions.explanation: IAA is the main natural auxin.

questions.q: The bending of a shoot towards light occurs because auxin accumulates on the
questions.explanation: Greater elongation of the shaded side bends the shoot toward the light.

questions.q: The primary root of a seedling growing downward into the soil shows
questions.explanation: Growth towards gravity is positive geotropism.

questions.q: The initial uptake of water by a dry seed, which makes it swell, takes place by
questions.explanation: Imbibition by colloids such as proteins and cellulose drives initial water uptake.

questions.q: Spraying sugarcane crops with a growth regulator increases the stem length and hence the sugar yield. The regulator is
questions.explanation: Gibberellins promote stem elongation in sugarcane.

questions.q: Differentiate between arithmetic and geometric growth.
questions.answer: In arithmetic growth only one daughter cell keeps dividing and the other matures, so growth is linear and the curve is a straight line. In geometric growth both daughter cells divide, so growth is exponential at first.
keyPoints: Arithmetic: one cell divides, linear plot
Root elongation at constant rate is arithmetic
questions.explanation: The geometric curve is sigmoid in the full period.

questions.q: What is seed dormancy? Mention two causes and a method of breaking it.
questions.answer: Dormancy is a period when a viable seed does not germinate even with suitable conditions. Causes: a hard impermeable seed coat, an immature embryo, or germination inhibitors like ABA. Methods: scarification of the coat, stratification, or treatment with gibberellins.
keyPoints: Two causes such as hard coat or inhibitors
A method such as scarification or gibberellin
questions.explanation: Dormancy helps seeds survive unfavourable conditions.

questions.q: The protein-digesting enzyme in gastric juice is
questions.explanation: Pepsin acts in the acidic medium of the stomach.

questions.q: The blood vessels that carry blood away from the heart are
questions.explanation: Arteries carry blood from the heart to the organs.

questions.q: The most abundant type of white blood cells (leucocytes) in human blood is
questions.explanation: Neutrophils form about 60 to 65 per cent of all WBCs.

questions.q: In an ECG, the QRS complex represents
questions.explanation: The QRS complex marks the depolarisation of the ventricles and the start of ventricular contraction.

questions.q: The rhythm centre of respiration, which controls the basic rate of breathing, lies in the
questions.explanation: The respiratory rhythm centre is in the medulla; the pneumotaxic centre in the pons moderates it.

questions.q: A person has a vital capacity of 4600 mL and a residual volume of 1200 mL. The total lung capacity is
questions.explanation: Total lung capacity = vital capacity + residual volume = 4600 + 1200 = 5800 mL.

questions.q: Write three differences between arteries and veins.
questions.answer: Arteries carry blood away from the heart, have thick elastic walls and have no valves; veins carry blood towards the heart, have thinner walls and have valves that prevent backflow.
questions.explanation: The pulmonary artery is an exception with deoxygenated blood.

questions.q: Explain how blood clots after an injury.
questions.answer: Injured tissue and platelets release thromboplastin, which activates a cascade that converts inactive prothrombin into thrombin in the presence of Ca2+. Thrombin changes soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin threads that trap blood cells, forming the clot.
keyPoints: Prothrombin changes to thrombin with calcium
Fibrinogen changes to fibrin forming the clot
questions.explanation: Clotting prevents excess blood loss.

questions.q: The central nervous system consists of
questions.explanation: The brain and spinal cord form the CNS.

questions.q: The hormone called the 'emergency hormone' or 'fight or flight hormone' is
questions.explanation: Adrenaline from the adrenal medulla prepares the body for stress.

questions.q: The neurotransmitter released at a neuromuscular junction is
questions.explanation: Acetylcholine triggers muscle fibre contraction.

questions.q: During contraction of a muscle fibre, the band that retains its length is the
questions.explanation: The A bands remain the same while the I bands shorten as thin filaments slide inwards.

questions.q: The hormone that stimulates the ejection of milk from the mammary glands is
questions.explanation: Oxytocin causes contraction of smooth muscle and milk ejection; prolactin stimulates milk production.

questions.q: In haemodialysis, nitrogenous wastes leave the blood because the dialysing fluid
options: is hot enough to burn them
has the same composition as plasma but no nitrogenous wastes
questions.explanation: Wastes diffuse down the concentration gradient into the dialysing fluid.

questions.q: Describe the sliding filament theory of muscle contraction in brief.
questions.answer: A nerve impulse releases Ca2+ in the muscle fibre; Ca2+ binds troponin and exposes the myosin-binding sites on actin. Myosin heads bind and pull the thin filaments towards the centre of the sarcomere using ATP, shortening the sarcomere.
keyPoints: Myosin heads bind actin and pull
questions.explanation: Filaments slide past each other; they do not shorten.

questions.q: Why does a person with diabetes insipidus pass a large volume of dilute urine?
questions.answer: The condition arises from a lack of ADH or of response to it, so the distal tubule and collecting duct do not reabsorb enough water. A large volume of dilute urine is lost and the person feels very thirsty.
questions.explanation: Diabetes insipidus is different from diabetes mellitus, where blood sugar is high.
